articles.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
articles.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
body: Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".
India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

articles.title: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder
articles.summary: The pregnant student was murdered after leaving a hotel with a journalist she had contacted to discuss her affair with the governor.
body: It is rare for such a high-ranking official to face public criminal trials in Kenya
A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about".
Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams said they would appeal against the sentence.
His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.
The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.
Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.
She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.
Otieno, 26, was killed between 3 and 4 September 2018 after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.
She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. The two were abducted shortly afterwards.
Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of a moving vehicle. His account of the abduction became a crucial lead in the investigation.
Otieno's body was later found near Kodera Forest.
A post-mortem examination found that she had died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.
The court also established that Obado was the biological father of her unborn child.
Obado and his co-accused were convicted of murder on 23 July 2026, following a lengthy trial in which prosecutors called 42 witnesses and presented 81 exhibits.
On Friday, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.
Before sentencing, Otieno's mother had appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, saying his imprisonment would amount to "another death in the family".
She urged the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, arguing that Otieno's three children, from different relationships, needed his support.
But the judge said the family's circumstances could not override the court's responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.
Otieno's family, through their lawyer Antony Opondo, told Kenya's Daily Nation that they would file an appeal seeking Obado's acquittal.
Otieno's murder sparked protests and renewed public debate about violence against women in Kenya.
A national survey found that at least 34% of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.
The case has also drawn attention because it is rare for such senior political figures to face public criminal trials in Kenya.
Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya, switching allegiance between a smaller political party and the region's dominant opposition movement.
He later backed President William Ruto and formally joined his ruling party in 2023, becoming a regional organiser.

articles.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
articles.summary: Erin Patterson is serving life in prison for poisoning her relatives with a toxic mushroom lunch in 2023.
body: Patterson was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives
Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.
Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".
She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.
Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.
She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.
She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.
Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

articles.title: Venezuela to scrap law that bars opposition from public office
articles.summary: The legislation has been criticised for enabling political persecution since it was introduced two years ago.
body: Jorge Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to the law's provisions
Venezuela will repeal a law that bars opposition figures from assuming public office, the speaker of the National Assembly Jorge Rodríguez has said.
The legislation, which was introduced two years ago, has been criticised for enabling political persecution, but Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to its provisions.
The older brother of Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez said he expected the reforms to be approved next week.
Delcy Rodríguez's interim government has been negotiating with opposition parties since taking over at the start of the year, when former President Nicolás Maduro was seized by the United States.
The legislation, known as the Simón Bolívar Law, was passed shortly after the election in July 2024 in which then-incumbent Maduro was declared the winner amid widespread allegations of fraud.
Under the legislation, individuals who requested or supported foreign sanctions against Venezuela were permanently banned from political office and had their assets confiscated.
"Legislative processes are dynamic processes. That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through," Jorge Rodríguez said.

During subsequent talks, which began in August, the interim government and parts of the opposition agreed to review several other laws as part of a "route map towards democracy", according to an opposition statement.
Delcy Rodríguez has promised that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election despite being excluded from transition talks.
Machado returned to the country in October after more than 10 months in exile.
In the 2024 election, Machado's ally Edmundo González ran in her place after she was barred from running for office by Maduro's government.
The electoral authority, which was closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.
The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.

articles.title: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall
articles.summary: Aid for Ukraine was among the disputes as EU members hope to conclude talks by the end of the year.
body: Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to reduce EU spending
European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.
Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.

Divisions were largely split along the lines of countries, including France and Italy, wanting to approve a higher-spending proposal against those advocating for financial restraint, with Germany chief among them.
Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.
Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget.
"I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters.
"The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council.
EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending.
Those advocating higher spending want the funds to future-proof industries such as farming and invest in regional development. Fiscally cautious countries want to avoid amassing ballooning debt.
Thursday's talks were set up by the European Council to unblock the impasse, with a proposal to reduce spending by approximately €220bn to €230bn.
Under the current proposal, the budget totals €1.582tn, which includes €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing.
Four countries wanting to rein in the budget, including Denmark and Austria, walked out of negotiations after several hours of meetings.

Merz said there was "new movement" towards reducing the size of the EU budget, though he added "we are not there yet" when he confirmed that a new round of negotiations would not take place in Brussels on Friday.
European budgets requires approval from all 27 countries, with each country effectively holding veto power.
French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to lower long-term spending.

France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".
Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency.

Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected."
Once the talks concluded, the European Council announced a two-day summit on 17 and 18 December would revive budget negotiations.
Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos was also named as the next President of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027.

articles.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
articles.summary: The Ugandan army is helping the Congolese military fight an Islamist militant group in the east of the country.
body: The planned withdrawal will end Uganda's nearly two-year campaign against ADF militants in Lubero
Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from a town in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours.
The troops will hand over security in Lubero, in North Kivu province, to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations, the Ugandan army said in a statement on Friday.

The announcement comes days after DR Congo summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over controversial social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni.
The Ugandan military did not give a reason for the withdrawal or say whether it was linked to the diplomatic row.
What are Ugandan forces doing in DR Congo?

The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) Islamist group fleeing joint military operations elsewhere in eastern DR Congo.
The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, is affiliated to the Islamic State and has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries.
Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign in November 2021, following a series of bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said that the joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, would continue elsewhere in DR Congo.
The planned withdrawal applies only to Lubero town.

Five years into the joint offensive, the ADF remains DR Congo's deadliest armed group, despite a significant decline in its activities in Uganda, according to the conflict monitoring organisation Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled).
John Ngono, Acled's DR Congo analyst, said the group was killing an average of four civilians a day and had expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo.
He said the findings suggested that "Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC".

Acled says the group has not carried out an attack in Uganda since June 2025, but its growing interest in mineral resources in DR Congo could help finance its operations and sustain its ability to threaten both countries.
The planned withdrawal comes amid strained relations between Uganda and DR Congo, despite years of close military co-operation.

Earlier this week, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to endorse a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo, threatening that Ugandan troops would seize it themselves if the rebels failed to do so.
The Congolese foreign ministry described his remarks as "particularly serious" and demanded that Uganda clarify its official position and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Gen Kainerugaba also defended Uganda's military presence in eastern DR Congo, insisting it was driven by security concerns.
The planned withdrawal comes amid renewed fighting between Congolese forces and rebels in the wider Lubero territory, raising fresh concerns about the safety of civilians.
Eastern DR Congo has endured decades of conflict involving dozens of armed groups, with millions of people forced to flee their homes.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
articles.summary: The announcement comes a year after a military coup with its leaders promising a return to civilian rule within 12 months.
body: Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam said the postponement was driven by factors including final reasons
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.summary: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.
body: Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.
Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.
In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".
His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".
Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.
Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs
Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."
Sir Rod Stewart, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, paid tribute to his "dear pal".
"We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun," Sir Rod posted on Instagram.
Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse Macabre
Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.
Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.
They became so popular in the States that the press labeled them the leaders of a "Second British Invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.
During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.
Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980s
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982
"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.
"His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.
"There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days."
Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982.
"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first," she wrote in her statement.
"Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
She continued: "Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life.
"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."
Duran Duran drummer quits band due to tinnitus
Duran Duran voted into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame

articles.title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
articles.summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.
body: Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation
Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.
Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

articles.title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
articles.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.
body: Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.
"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".
Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.
Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.
Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.
Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.
Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.
The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.
Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.
The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.
Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
articles.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
body: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Sheikh Hasina: The pro-democracy icon who became an autocrat
Hasina's conviction for crimes against humanity is testing India-Bangladesh ties
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India, his neighbour, since becoming prime minister in February

Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).
Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.
Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.

articles.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
articles.summary: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
body: Watch: Man wrongly sentenced to death says Met Police ruined his life

A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.
David and Judith Tebbutt were on a dream holiday to Kenya when they were attacked

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.
Ali Kololo says he lost contact with his children while he was in prison

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.
Neil Hibberd retired from the police in 2017

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."
Additional reporting by Ed Habershon

articles.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
articles.summary: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.
body: Twin sisters Romina (left) and Taraneh Rahimi were arrested in late January, their cousin says
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.
She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.
He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.
He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.
Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.
January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution
The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".
The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.
Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin says

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.
Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".
Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.
This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups
Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.
Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.
"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.
The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.
The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."
Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say
Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".
At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".
Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".
Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".
In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".
Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured
Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.
Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."
Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.
Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.
Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.
Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.
Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

articles.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
articles.summary: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.
body: Protests on the streets of France over students' concerns and the cost of living have been marked by looting and unrest in recent weeks
France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027, unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.

With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.
In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.
That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.
But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.
"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."
On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.

His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.
The protests started as an expression of anger at conditions in high schools

In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).
Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.

So with the soft-left emasculated, the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right. But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom.
"A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper. "But it is looking increasingly probable."

In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote. Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.

Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling. They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal; the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau; and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.
David Lisnard (centre) has seen membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie jump to more than 100,000

Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.

But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.

According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists. Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum.
"The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns. In the middle… nothing."
Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap.
"In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions. We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says.
"What do we have in between? Arguments about names and polling figures and whether or not there should be a primary. It's not, to put it mildly, an encouraging start."

For Fressoz, "There is no-one in the centre who is taking up the fight. When Le Pen makes her proposals about pensions, there is no-one saying, 'Hang on, that doesn't add up!'. Macron – who did after all take her on and beat her – is said to be furious."

Any mention of Macron, though, is most unwelcome for the camp that nominally is his heir. Philippe, Attal and Retailleau all served under a president who Baverez now calls "as toxic as Trump", so deep is his unpopularity in the country. Lisnard, by contrast, makes much of his refusal to serve under Macron – but he faces another handicap.

According to Fressoz, "Lisnard has shot up in the polls because he is on the right of the right, and there is always an appetite for a figure who is not Le Pen, but who speaks her kind of language on immigration.
"But Lisnard is an economic liberal, and in France that is a minority taste. He'll have his moment but then he will deflate."
Emmanuel Macron is now considered a politically toxic figure in France

With five months to go to until the election, all is not lost for the mainstream. Optimists in its ranks say that come the new year, opinion polls will start settling behind one or other centre-right candidate, and the others will feel obliged to step aside.

Talk of a centre-right primary – as occurred ahead of the 2017 election – is beginning to ebb. The two strongest candidates, Philippe and Lisnard, are opposed. Lisnard says he supports one but his conditions are designed to be unacceptable to the rest. Retailleau and Attal are in favour – but that, says Tabard, is "mainly as a way to keep their hopes alive."

In theory then it is possible a name will emerge in January or February, and start pulling behind him (or less likely, her) the mass of voters who do not want a disruptive radical as France's next head of state.
Possible, but hardly a good bet.
For Fressoz of Le Monde, "After years of Macron's 'neither left nor right', the left and right are once again shaping French politics. But now it is the extremes who are in control."

Le Pen and Mélenchon have both already run three times for the presidency. Their visions were defined long ago, their strategies laid, their activists trained. Polarisation is their friend, so is the social tension of recent weeks, and both are undisputed masters in their own camps.
The 2027 dénouement has been in their sights for years. That is their massive advantage.
